go:422786.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 1
go:422786.question:
If ' $\rightarrow$ ' denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words

[dry $\rightarrow$ arid $\rightarrow$ parched] is analogous to [diet $\rightarrow$ fast $\rightarrow$ ________ ].

Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?

  1. starve
  2. reject
  3. feast 
  4. deny

detailed_solution.markdown: dry $\rightarrow$ arid $\rightarrow$ parched: increasing degree of lack of water. diet $\rightarrow$ fast $\rightarrow$ ___ : increasing degree of not eating. Next stronger level is starve. (reject, feast, deny do not fit the scale.)

go:422785.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 2
go:422785.question:
​​​If two distinct non-zero real variables $x$ and $y$ are such that $(x+y)$ is proportional to $(x-y)$ then the value of $\frac{x}{y}$

  1. depends on $x y$
  2. depends only on $x$ and not on $y$
  3. depends only on $y$ and not on $x$
  4. is a constant

detailed_solution.markdown:
$x+y=k(x-y)$ for a constant $k$.

$x+y=kx-ky\Rightarrow y(1+k)=x(k-1)\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{y}=\dfrac{k+1}{k-1}$

This depends only on $k$, so it is a constant.

go:422784.question:

go:422783.question:
​​​​The number of coins of ₹$1$, ₹$5$, and ₹$10$ denominations that a person has are in the ratio $5:3:13$. Of the total amount, the percentage of money in ₹$5$ coins is

  1. $21 \%$
  2. $14 \frac{2}{7} \%$
  3. $10 \%$
  4. $30 \%$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Let coins be $5k,3k,13k$.

Money: Rs.1 $\rightarrow$ $5k$, Rs.5 $\rightarrow$ $15k$, Rs.10 $\rightarrow$ $130k$. Total $=150k$.

Share of Rs.5 coins $=\dfrac{15k}{150k}\times100=10\%$

go:422782.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 5
go:422782.question:
For positive non-zero real variables $p$ and $q$, if

$\log \left(p^2+q^2\right)=\log p+\log q+2 \log 3,$

then, the value of $\frac{p^4+q^4}{p^2 q^2}$ is

  1. $79$
  2. $81$
  3. $9$
  4. $83$

detailed_solution.markdown:
$\log(p^2+q^2)=\log(9pq)\Rightarrow p^2+q^2=9pq$

Squaring: $p^4+q^4+2p^2q^2=81p^2q^2\Rightarrow p^4+q^4=79p^2q^2$

$\dfrac{p^4+q^4}{p^2q^2}=79$

go:422780.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 7
go:422780.question:
​​A rectangular paper sheet of dimensions $54 \mathrm{~cm} \times 4 \mathrm{~cm}$ is taken. The two longer edges of the sheet are joined together to create a cylindrical tube. A cube whose surface area is equal to the area of the sheet is also taken.

Then, the ratio of the volume of the cylindrical tube to the volume of the cube is

  1. $1 / \pi$
  2. $2 / \pi$
  3. $3 / \pi$
  4. $4 / \pi$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Joining the longer (54 cm) edges gives a tube of height 54 and circumference 4.

$2\pi r=4\Rightarrow r=\dfrac{2}{\pi}$, $V_{cyl}=\pi r^2h=\pi\cdot\dfrac{4}{\pi^2}\cdot54=\dfrac{216}{\pi}$

Cube: $6a^2=54\times4=216\Rightarrow a=6$, $V_{cube}=216$

Ratio $=\dfrac{216/\pi}{216}=\dfrac{1}{\pi}$

go:422779.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 8
go:422779.question:
The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical $2,000\; \mathrm{kcal}$ diet of a person.

The typical energy density $(\mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{g})$ of these macronutrients is given in the table.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline
\text{Macronutrient} & \text{Energy density (kcal/g)}  \\  \hline
\text{Carbohydrates} & \text{4}  \\  \hline
\text{Proteins} & \text{4}  \\  \hline \text{Unsaturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Saturated fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline \text{Trans fat} & \text{9}  \\  \hline
\end{array}$$

The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is 

  1. $44.4$
  2. $77.8$
  3. $100$
  4. $3,600$

detailed_solution.markdown:
From the pie chart, fats = unsaturated 20% + saturated 20% + trans 5% = 45%.

Energy from fat $=0.45\times2000=900$ kcal.

All fats give 9 kcal/g, so fat $=900/9=100$ g.

go:422778.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 9
go:422778.question:
A rectangular paper of $20 \mathrm{~cm} \times 8 \mathrm{~cm}$ is folded $3$ times. Each fold is made along the line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final folded sheet (in $\mathrm{cm}$ ) is

  1. $18$
  2. $24$
  3. $20$
  4. $21$

detailed_solution.markdown: Each fold halves the current longer side. - 20 $\times$ 8 $\rightarrow$ fold $\rightarrow$ 10 $\times$ 8 - 10 $\times$ 8 $\rightarrow$ fold $\rightarrow$ 5 $\times$ 8 (now 8 is the longer side) - 5 $\times$ 8 $\rightarrow$ fold $\rightarrow$ 5 $\times$ 4 Perimeter $=2(5+4)=18$ cm.

go:422777.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | GA Question: 10
go:422777.question:
​​The least number of squares to be added in the figure to make $\text{A B}$ a line of symmetry is

  1. $6$
  2. $4$
  3. $5$
  4. $7$

detailed_solution.markdown:
For AB to be a line of symmetry, every square must have its mirror image on the other side of AB.

- Left figure: 1 square above AB and 2 squares below (one just below the line on the left, one two rows down on the right). None of them has its mirror image $\rightarrow$ add 3.

- Right figure: 3 squares, all below AB $\rightarrow$ add their 3 mirror images above.

Total $=3+3=6$

go:422841.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 1
go:422841.question:
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x)=\max \left\{x, x^3\right\}, x \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where $f(x)$ is NOT differentiable is

  1. $\{-1,1,2\}$
  2. $\{-2,-1,1\}$
  3. $\{0,1\}$
  4. $\{-1,0,1\}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Compare $x$ and $x^3$: they are equal at $x=-1,0,1$. So

$f(x)=x$ for $x\le -1$, $x^3$ on $[-1,0]$, $x$ on $[0,1]$, $x^3$ for $x\ge1$.

At every switching point the two pieces have different slopes ($\frac{d}{dx}x=1$, $\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2$):

- $x=-1$: slopes $1$ and $3$ $\rightarrow$ corner

- $x=0$: slopes $0$ and $1$ $\rightarrow$ corner

- $x=1$: slopes $1$ and $3$ $\rightarrow$ corner

Everywhere else $f$ is a polynomial, hence differentiable.

go:422840.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 2
go:422840.question:
The product of all eigenvalues of the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{array}\right]$ is

  1. $-1$
  2. $0$
  3. $1$
  4. $2$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Product of all eigenvalues $=\det(A)$.

$\det(A)=1(45-48)-2(36-42)+3(32-35)=-3+12-9=0$

(Quick check: $R_1+R_3=2R_2$, so the rows are dependent and the matrix is singular.)

go:422839.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 3
go:422839.question:
Consider a system that uses $5$ bits for representing signed integers in $2$ 's complement format. In this system, two integers $A$ and $B$ are represented as $A$=$01010$ and $B$=$11010$. Which one of the following operations will result in either an arithmetic overflow or an arithmetic underflow?

  1. $A+B$
  2. $A-B$
  3. $B-A$
  4. $2 * B$

detailed_solution.markdown: With 5-bit 2's complement the range is $-16$ to $+15$. $A=01010=+10$, $B=11010=-6$. - $A+B=4$ $\rightarrow$ fits - $A-B=10+6=16$ $\rightarrow$ exceeds +15, overflow - $B-A=-16$ $\rightarrow$ fits (lowest value) - $2B=-12$ $\rightarrow$ fits

go:422838.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 4
go:422838.question:
Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of $\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\}$ for some $n \geq 4$. Let $X$ be the event that $1$ occurs before $2$ in the permutation, and $Y$ the event that $3$ occurs before $4$. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. The events $X$ and $Y$ are mutually exclusive
  2. The events $X$ and $Y$ are independent
  3. Either event $X$ or $Y$ must occur
  4. Event $X$ is more likely than event $Y$

detailed_solution.markdown: By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so $P(X)=\frac12$; similarly $P(Y)=\frac12$. The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so $P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)$ $\rightarrow$ independent. - Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 $\ldots$ satisfies both. - Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 $\ldots$ satisfies none. - Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y.

go:422837.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 5
go:422837.question:
​​​​Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

  1. In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O device and main memory in a stolen cycle
  2. For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the cycle stealing mode
  3. Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven I/O mechanism
  4. The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Cycle stealing: DMA takes one bus cycle and moves one word $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block (no repeated bus requests), so it has higher throughput for bulk transfer $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt-driven I/O $\text{---}$ FALSE. In programmed I/O the CPU keeps polling the device status and wastes cycles; interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device interrupts. - Vectored interrupts give the ISR address directly (no polling to find the device), so ISR starts faster $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:422836.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 6
go:422836.question:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.

  1. HTTP GET request for the index page
  2. DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
  3. HTTP GET request for an image object
  4. TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server

Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer?

  1. $\text{(iv), (ii), (iii), (i)}$
  2. $\text{(ii), (iv), (iii), (i)}$
  3. $\text{(ii), (iv), (i), (iii)}$
  4. $\text{(iv), (ii), (i), (iii)}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Order in which the packets leave the computer: 1. (ii) DNS request $\text{---}$ the IP address of the server is needed before anything else (caches are empty). 2. (iv) TCP SYN $\text{---}$ open the TCP connection with the server. 3. (i) GET index page $\text{---}$ first request on the connection. 4. (iii) GET image $\text{---}$ the browser knows about the image only after it receives and parses the index page.

go:422835.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 7
go:422835.question:
Given an integer array of size $N$, we want to check if the array is sorted (in either ascending or descending order). An algorithm solves this problem by making a single pass through the array and comparing each element of the array only with its adjacent elements. The worst-case time complexity of this algorithm is

  1. both $\mathrm{O}(N)$ and $\Omega(N)$
  2. $\mathrm{O}(N)$ but $\operatorname{not} \Omega(N)$
  3. $\Omega(N)$ but not $\mathrm{O}(N)$ 
  4. neither $\mathrm{O}(N)$ nor $\Omega(N)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
The algorithm compares each pair of adjacent elements once: $N-1$ comparisons in the worst case (when the array is actually sorted, it must check every pair before saying YES).

It cannot do less: any element not examined could break the order. So the worst case is $\Theta(N)$, i.e. both $O(N)$ and $\Omega(N)$.

go:422834.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 8
go:422834.question:
Consider the following $\mathrm{C}$ program:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {

int a=6;

int b = 0;

while (a<10)   {

a = a / 12+1 ;

a += b ;}

printf ("%d", a);

return 0 ; }

Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. The program prints $9$ as output
  2. The program prints $10$ as output
  3. The program gets stuck in an infinite loop
  4. The program prints $6$ as output

detailed_solution.markdown:
Integer division is used.

Iteration 1: $a=6/12+1=0+1=1$, then $a=a+b=1+0=1$.

Iteration 2: $a=1/12+1=0+1=1$ again, and so on.

$a$ is stuck at 1, so the condition $a \lt 10$ is always true and printf is never reached.

go:422833.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 9
go:422833.question:
​​​Consider the following $\mathrm{C}$ program:

#include <stdio.h>
void fX();

int main() {
    fX();
    return 0;
}

void fX() {
    char a;
    if ((a = getchar()) != '\n')
        fX();
    if (a != '\n')
        putchar(a);
}

Assume that the input to the program from the command line is $1234$ followed by a newline character. Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?

  1. The program will not terminate
  2. The program will terminate with no output
  3. The program will terminate with $4321$ as output
  4. The program will terminate with $1234$ as output

detailed_solution.markdown: Each call of fX() reads one character and, if it is not newline, calls fX() again before printing. Each call has its own local $a$. Calls read: '1' $\rightarrow$ '2' $\rightarrow$ '3' $\rightarrow$ '4' $\rightarrow$ '\n'. The last call reads newline, makes no further call and prints nothing. While returning, the calls print their characters in reverse order: 4, 3, 2, 1. Then main returns normally.

go:422832.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 10
go:422832.question:
Let $\mathrm{S}$ be the specification: "Instructors teach courses. Students register for courses. Courses are allocated classrooms. Instructors guide students." Which one of the following $\mathrm{ER}$ diagrams CORRECTLY represents $\mathrm{S}$? 

  1. $\text{(i)}$
  2. $\text{(ii)}$
  3. $\text{(iii)}$
  4. $\text{(iv)}$

detailed_solution.markdown: From the specification we need 4 entity sets $\text{---}$ Instructor, Course, Student, Classroom $\text{---}$ and 4 relationships: Instructor-Teaches-Course, Student-Registers-Course, Course-Allocated-Classroom, Instructor-Guides-Student. - (i): Registration is drawn as an entity and Student as a relationship $\text{---}$ wrong. - (ii): no Student entity; an extra Projects entity is used $\text{---}$ wrong. - (iii): Classroom is attached directly to Course and the Allocation relationship does not connect Classroom $\text{---}$ wrong. - (iv): all four entities and all four relationships are connected correctly.

go:422831.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 11
go:422831.question:
In a $\mathrm{B}^+$ tree, the requirement of at least half-full $(50 \%)$ node occupancy is relaxed for which one of the following cases?

  1. Only the root node
  2. All leaf nodes
  3. All internal nodes
  4. Only the leftmost leaf node

detailed_solution.markdown: In a B+ tree of order $m$, every node (internal or leaf) must be at least half full $\text{---}$ except the root. The root can have as few as 2 children (or just 1 key if it is a leaf), otherwise a small tree could never be built.

go:422830.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 12
go:422830.question:
Which of the following statements about a relation $\mathbf{R}$ in first normal form $\text{(1NF)}$ is/are TRUE?

  1. $\mathbf{R}$ can have a multi-attribute key
  2. $\mathbf{R}$ cannot have a foreign key
  3. $\mathbf{R}$ cannot have a composite attribute
  4. $\mathbf{R}$ cannot have more than one candidate key

detailed_solution.markdown: 1NF only requires every attribute value to be atomic (no multi-valued or composite attributes). - R can have a multi-attribute key $\text{---}$ TRUE (e.g. key (roll_no, course_id)). This is about keys, not about values. - R cannot have a foreign key $\text{---}$ FALSE, 1NF puts no restriction on foreign keys. - R cannot have a composite attribute $\text{---}$ TRUE, a composite attribute is non-atomic and must be split into simple attributes. - R cannot have more than one candidate key $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:422829.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 13
go:422829.question:
​Let $L_1, L_2$ be two regular languages and $L_3$ a language which is not regular.

Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

  1. $L_1=L_2$ if and only if $L_1 \cap \overline{L_2}=\phi$
  2. $L_1 \cup L_3$ is not regular
  3. $\overline{L_3}$ is not regular 
  4. $\overline{L_1} \cup \overline{L_2}$ is regular

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi$ only means $L_1\subseteq L_2$. Equality also needs $L_2\subseteq L_1$ $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- $L_1\cup L_3$ can be regular: take $L_1=\Sigma^*$, then $L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*$ $\text{---}$ FALSE (not always).

- If $\overline{L_3}$ were regular, then its complement $L_3$ would be regular (closure under complement). So $\overline{L_3}$ is not regular $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so $\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}$ is regular $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:422828.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 14
go:422828.question:
Which of the following statements about threads is/are TRUE?

  1. Threads can only be implemented in kernel space
  2. Each thread has its own file descriptor table for open files
  3. All the threads belonging to a process share a common stack
  4. Threads belonging to a process are by default not protected from each other

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- Threads can also be implemented in user space (user-level threads) $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- The file descriptor table belongs to the process and is shared by all its threads $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- Every thread has its own stack (and registers, PC) $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- Threads share the same address space, so one thread can read/overwrite another thread's data; there is no protection between them $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:422827.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 15
go:422827.question:
Which of the following process state transitions is/are NOT possible?

  1. Running to Ready
  2. Waiting to Running
  3. Ready to Waiting
  4. Running to Terminated

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Running $\rightarrow$ Ready: possible (preemption / time slice over). - Waiting $\rightarrow$ Running: NOT possible. When the I/O finishes, the process goes to Ready; only the scheduler can move it to Running. - Ready $\rightarrow$ Waiting: NOT possible. A process can block (request I/O) only while it is running. - Running $\rightarrow$ Terminated: possible (exit).

go:422826.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 16
go:422826.question:
Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?

  1. Shift-reduce Parser
  2. Predictive Parser
  3. LL$(1)$ Parser 
  4. LR Parser

detailed_solution.markdown: Bottom-up parsers build the parse tree from the leaves up to the root using reductions: shift-reduce parsers, operator precedence parser and the LR family (LR(0), SLR, LALR, CLR). Predictive parser and LL(1) parser are top-down parsers.

go:422825.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 17
go:422825.question:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two events in a probability space with $P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5$, and $P(A \cap B)=0.1$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. The two events $A$ and $B$ are independent
  2. $P(A \cup B)=0.7$
  3. $P\left(A \cap B^c\right)=0.2$, where $B^c$ is the complement of the event $B$ 
  4. $P\left(A^c \cap B^c\right)=0.4$, where $A^c$ and $B^c$ are the complements of the events $A$ and $B$, respectively

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- Independence: $P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1$ $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- $P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- $P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=0.3-0.1=0.2$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- $P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A\cup B)=0.3\ne0.4$ $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:422824.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 18
go:422824.question:
​​Consider the circuit shown below where the gates may have propagation delays. Assume that all signal transitions occur instantaneously and that wires have no delays. Which of the following statements about the circuit is/are CORRECT?

  1. With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic Zero
  2. With no propagation delays, the output $Y$ is always logic One
  3. With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic One after $X$ transitions from logic Zero to logic One
  4. With propagation delays, the output $Y$ can have a transient logic Zero after $X$ transitions from logic One to logic Zero

detailed_solution.markdown: The circuit computes $Y=X\cdot\overline{X}$. - No delays: $X\cdot\overline{X}=0$ always $\rightarrow$ Y is always 0 (option 1 TRUE, option 2 FALSE). - X goes 0 $\rightarrow$ 1: the AND gate sees X = 1 immediately, but the NOT output is still 1 until its delay passes. For that short time both inputs are 1, so Y gives a transient 1 (glitch) $\text{---}$ TRUE. - X goes 1 $\rightarrow$ 0: the direct input becomes 0 immediately, so Y stays 0 no matter what the NOT output does $\text{---}$ no transient, FALSE.

go:422823.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 19
go:422823.question:
​$\mathrm{TCP}$ client $\mathrm{P}$ successfully establishes a connection to $\text{TCP}$ server $\mathrm{Q}$. Let $\text{N}_{P}$ denote the sequence number in the $\text{SYN}$ sent from $\mathrm{P}$ to $\mathrm{Q}$. Let $\text{N}_{Q}$ denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from $\text{Q}$ to $\text{P}$. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

  1. The sequence number $\text{N}_{P}$ is chosen randomly by $\mathrm{P}$
  2. The sequence number $\text{N}_{P}$ is always $0$ for a new connection
  3. The acknowledgement number $\text{N}_{Q}$ is equal to $\text{N}_{P}$ 
  4. The acknowledgement number $\text{N}_{Q}$ is equal to $\text{N}_{P}+1$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly (to avoid confusion with old segments and for security) $\text{---}$ TRUE; it is not always 0.

- A SYN segment consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges with the next expected number: $N_Q=N_P+1$ $\text{---}$ TRUE (so $N_Q=N_P$ is false).

go:422822.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 20
go:422822.question:
Consider a $5$-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?

  1. In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction
  2. In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the input of the EX stage of the next instruction
  3. Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls
  4. Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the pipeline stages

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Option 1: this is exactly the definition of forwarding (bypassing) $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Option 2: a value available at the output of MEM (e.g. a loaded value) can be fed to the EX input of a later instruction $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Option 3: forwarding cannot remove every stall. Example: load followed immediately by an instruction using the loaded value still needs 1 stall (load-use hazard) $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Option 4: forwarding needs extra hardware (extra paths, multiplexers, hazard detection logic) $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:422821.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 21
go:422821.question:
Which of the following fields is/are modified in the $\text{IP}$ header of a packet going out of a network address translation $\text{(NAT)}$ device from an internal network to an external network?

  1. Source $\text{IP}$
  2. Destination $\text{IP}$
  3. Header Checksum
  4. Total Length

detailed_solution.markdown: For an outgoing packet, NAT replaces the private source IP (and port) with its public IP. Because a header field changed, the header checksum must be recomputed. Destination IP is unchanged (it is the outside server), and total length is unchanged (payload size is the same).

go:422820.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 22
go:422820.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be non-empty finite sets such that there exist one-to-one and onto functions $\text{(i)}$ from $A$ to $B$ and $\text{(ii)}$ from $A \times A$ to $A \cup B$. The number of possible values of $\text{|A|}$ is ___________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Bijection $A\to B$ $\Rightarrow$ $|A|=|B|=n$.

Bijection $A\times A\to A\cup B$ $\Rightarrow$ $n^2=|A\cup B|$.

But $n\le|A\cup B|\le 2n$, so $n\le n^2\le 2n$ $\Rightarrow$ $n\le2$.

- $n=1$: $A=B$, $|A\cup B|=1=1^2$ True

- $n=2$: take A and B disjoint, $|A\cup B|=4=2^2$ True

So $|A|\in\{1,2\}$.

go:422819.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 23
go:422819.question:
Consider the operator precedence and associativity rules for the integer arithmetic operators given in the table below. $$\begin{array}{|c|l|}\hline \textbf{Operator}  &  \textbf{Precedence} & \textbf{Associativity} \\\hline  \text{$+$} & \text{Highest} & \text{Left} \\\hline  \text{$-$} & \text{High} & \text{Right} \\\hline  \text{$*$} & \text{Medium} & \text{Right}  \\\hline \text{$/$} & \text{Low} & \text{Right}  \\\hline \end{array}$$

The value of the expression $3+1+5 * 2 / 7+2-4-7-6 / 2$ as per the above rules is ________.

detailed_solution.markdown: Precedence: + (highest) $\gt$ $-$ $\gt$ * $\gt$ / (lowest). The lowest-precedence operator is applied last, so / splits the expression: $(3+1+5*2)\;/\;(7+2-4-7-6)\;/\;2$ First part: + binds before *, so $(3+1+5)*2=9*2=18$. Second part: + first: $7+2=9$. Then $-$ is right associative: $9-(4-(7-6))=9-(4-1)=6$. / is right associative: $18/(6/2)=18/3=6$.

go:422818.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 24
go:422818.question: The number of spanning trees in a complete graph of $4$ vertices labelled $\text{A, B, C,}$ and $\text{D}$ is _________.

Number of spanning trees of a complete graph $K_n$ (Cayley's formula) $=n^{n-2}$.

$4^{4-2}=16$

go:422816.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 26
go:422816.question:
Consider a network path $\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R}$ between nodes $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ via router $\mathrm{Q}$. Node $\mathrm{P}$ sends a file of size $10^6$ bytes to $\text{R}$ via this path by splitting the file into chunks of $10^3$ bytes each. Node $\text{P}$ sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the $\text{MTU}$.

Each of the links $\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}$ and $\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R}$ has a bandwidth of $10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec}$, and negligible propagation latency. Router $\text{Q}$ immediately transmits every packet it receives from $\text{P}$ to $\text{R}$, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router $\text{Q}$ can simultaneously receive on $\operatorname{link} \mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}$ and transmit on $\operatorname{link} \mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R}$.

Assume $\text{P}$ starts transmitting the chunks at time $t=0$.

Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to $3$ decimal places) at which $\mathrm{R}$ receives all the chunks of the file?

  1. $8.000$
  2. $8.008$
  3. $15.992$
  4. $16.000$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Number of chunks $=10^6/10^3=1000$. Each chunk $=8000$ bits, so transmission time on a link $=\frac{8000}{10^6}=8$ ms.

P sends the chunks back to back: the last chunk is fully sent by P at $1000\times8\text{ ms}=8$ s.

Q forwards each chunk while receiving the next, so only the last chunk adds one more transmission of 8 ms on Q-R.

Total $=8+0.008=8.008$ s.

go:422814.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 28
go:422814.question:
Consider the following grammar $G$, with $S$ as the start symbol. The grammar $G$ has three incomplete productions denoted by $(1), (2)$, and $(3)$.

$$\begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow d a T \mid \quad(1) \\ & T \rightarrow a S|b T| \quad(2) \\ & R \rightarrow(3) \mid \epsilon\end{aligned}$$

The set of terminals is $\{a, b, c, d, f\}$. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.

$\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{FIRST}(S)=\{c, d, f\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(T)=\{a, b, \epsilon\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(R)=\{c, \epsilon\} \\ & \operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)=\{c, f, \$\}, \operatorname{FOLLOW}(R)=\{f\}\end{aligned}$

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?

  1. (1) $S \rightarrow R f$ (2) $T \rightarrow \epsilon$ (3) $R \rightarrow c T R$
  2. (1) $S \rightarrow f R$ (2) $T \rightarrow \epsilon$ (3) $R \rightarrow c T R$
  3. (1) $S \rightarrow f R$ (2) $T \rightarrow c T$ (3) $R \rightarrow c R$
  4. (1) $S \rightarrow R f$ (2) $T \rightarrow c T$ (3) $R \rightarrow c R$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Use the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets:

- $FIRST(S)=\{c,d,f\}$ but $daT$ gives only d, so (1) must give c and f. $S\rightarrow Rf$ gives $(FIRST(R)-\epsilon)\cup\{f\}=\{c,f\}$ True ($S\rightarrow fR$ gives only f).

- $\epsilon\in FIRST(T)$, so (2) is $T\rightarrow\epsilon$.

- $FIRST(R)=\{c,\epsilon\}$, so (3) starts with c.

Check FOLLOW with $R\rightarrow cTR$: $FOLLOW(T)\supseteq FIRST(R)-\epsilon=\{c\}$ and $FOLLOW(R)=\{f\}$ (from $S\rightarrow Rf$); together with $ this gives $FOLLOW(S)=FOLLOW(T)=\{c,f,\$\}$ True. With $R\rightarrow cR$, c could never follow T.

go:422813.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 29
go:422813.question:
Consider the following pseudo-code.

L 1: t1 = -1

L 2: t2 = 0 

L 3: t3 = 0

L 4: t4 = 4 * t3

L 5: t5 = 4 * t2

L 6: t6 = t5 * M

L 7: t7 = t4 + t6

L 8: t8 = a[t7]

L 9: if t8 <= max goto L11

L 10: t1 = t8

L 11: t3 = t3 + 1

L 12: if t3 < M   goto L4

L 13: t2 = t2 + 1

L 14: if t2 < N goto L3

L 15: max = t1

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY specifies the number of basic blocks and the number of instructions in the largest basic block, respectively?

  1. $6$ and $6$
  2. $6$ and $7$
  3. $7$ and $7$
  4. $7$ and $6$

Basic blocks: - B1: L1-L2 (2) - B2: L3 (1) - B3: L4-L9 (6) - B4: L10 (1) - B5: L11-L12 (2) - B6: L13-L14 (2) - B7: L15 (1) 7 basic blocks; the largest (B3) has 6 instructions.

go:422812.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 30
go:422812.question:
​​​Consider the following two threads $\mathrm{T} 1$ and $\mathrm{T} 2$ that update two shared variables $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$. Assume that initially $\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{b}=1$. Though context switching between threads can happen at any time, each statement of  $\mathrm{T} 1$ or  $\mathrm{T} 2$ is executed atomically without interruption.

$\begin{gathered}\mathrm{T} 1 \\ \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{a}+1; \\ \mathrm{~b}=\mathrm{b}+1;\end{gathered}$ $\quad$ $\begin{gathered}\mathrm{T} 2 \\ \mathrm{b}=\mathrm {2 * b};  \\ \mathrm{a}=\mathrm 2 * {a}; \end{gathered}$

Which one of the following options lists all the possible combinations of values of a and b after both T1 and T2 finish execution?

  1. $(\mathrm{a}=4, \mathrm{~b}=4) ;(\mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=3) ;(\mathrm{a}=4, \mathrm{~b}=3)$
  2. $(\mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=4) ;(\mathrm{a}=4, \mathrm{~b}=3) ;(\mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=3)$
  3. $(\mathrm{a}=4, \mathrm{~b}=4) ;(\mathrm{a}=4, \mathrm{~b}=3) ;(\mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=4)$
  4. $(\mathrm{a}=2, \mathrm{~b}=2) ;(\mathrm{a}=2, \mathrm{~b}=3) ;(\mathrm{a}=3, \mathrm{~b}=4)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Final a depends only on which a-update runs first; final b only on which b-update runs first.

- a: $(1+1)\times2=4$ if T1's update is first, $2\times1+1=3$ otherwise.

- b: $(1+1)\times2=4$ if T1's update is first, $3$ otherwise.

- T1 then T2: (4, 4). T2 then T1: (3, 3).

- T1: a=a+1, T2: b=2b, T2: a=2a, T1: b=b+1 $\rightarrow$ (4, 3).

- (3, 4) is impossible: it needs T2's a-update before T1's a-update and T1's b-update before T2's b-update. But in program order T1 does a before b and T2 does b before a, so this creates a cycle.

go:422811.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 31
go:422811.question:
​​​​​An array $[82,101,90,11,111,75,33,131,44,93]$ is heapified. Which one of the following options represents the first three elements in the heapified array?

  1. $82,90,101$
  2. $82,11,93$
  3. $131,11,93$
  4. $131,111,90$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Build a max-heap bottom-up (heapify from index $\lfloor10/2\rfloor=5$ down to 1):

[82, 101, 90, 11, 111, 75, 33, 131, 44, 93]

- i=5 (111): child 93 $\rightarrow$ no change.

- i=4 (11): children 131, 44 $\rightarrow$ swap with 131.

- i=3 (90): children 75, 33 $\rightarrow$ no change.

- i=2 (101): children 131, 111 $\rightarrow$ swap with 131 (101 then fine above 11, 44).

- i=1 (82): swap with 131, then with 111, then with 93.

Heap: [131, 111, 90, 101, 93, 75, 33, 11, 44, 82]

go:422810.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 32
go:422810.question:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

$T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}\sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n})+n \text { for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 \quad \text { for } n=1\end{array}\right.$

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?

  1. $T(n)=\Theta(n \log \log n)$
  2. $T(n)=\Theta(n \log n)$
  3. $T(n)=\Theta\left(n^2 \log n\right)$
  4. $T(n)=\Theta\left(n^2 \log \log n\right)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Divide both sides by $n$: $\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1$.

Let $S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}$. Then $S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1$.

Taking square roots repeatedly, $n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots$ reaches a constant after $\log\log n$ steps, adding 1 each step. So $S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)$.

$T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)$

go:422809.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 33
go:422809.question:
Consider a binary min-heap containing $105$ distinct elements. Let $k$ be the index (in the underlying array) of the maximum element stored in the heap. The number of possible values of $k$ is

  1. $53$
  2. $52$
  3. $27$
  4. $1$

detailed_solution.markdown: In a min-heap every parent is smaller than its children, so the maximum element cannot have a child $\text{---}$ it must be a leaf. Any leaf can hold it. In an array heap of $n$ elements, leaves are at indices $\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$ to $n$. $n=105$: leaves are 53 to 105 $\rightarrow$ $105-52=53$ positions.

go:422808.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 34
go:422808.question:
​The symbol $\rightarrow$ indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?

  1. $(X, Y) \rightarrow(Z, W)$ implies $X \rightarrow(Z, W)$ 
  2. $(X, Y) \rightarrow(Z, W)$ implies $(X, Y) \rightarrow Z$
  3. $((X, Y) \rightarrow Z$ and $W \rightarrow Y)$ implies $(X, W) \rightarrow Z$
  4. $(X \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow Z)$ implies $X \rightarrow Z$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- $(X,Y)\rightarrow(Z,W)$ does not give $X\rightarrow(Z,W)$; Y may be required $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- Decomposition rule: $XY\rightarrow ZW$ $\Rightarrow$ $XY\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- Pseudo-transitivity: $W\rightarrow Y$ $\Rightarrow$ $XW\rightarrow XY$ (augment by X), and $XY\rightarrow Z$, so $XW\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- Transitivity: $X\rightarrow Y,\;Y\rightarrow Z$ $\Rightarrow$ $X\rightarrow Z$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:422807.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 35
go:422807.question:
​​​​Let $G$ be a directed graph and $T$ a depth first search $\text{(DFS)}$ spanning tree in $G$ that is rooted at a vertex $v$. Suppose $T$ is also a breadth first search $\text{(BFS)}$ tree in $G$, rooted at $v$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph $G$ and tree $T$?

  1. There are no back-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
  2. There are no cross-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
  3. There are no forward-edge in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
  4. The only edges in $G$ are the edges in $T$

detailed_solution.markdown: In a BFS tree, every edge $u\rightarrow w$ of G satisfies $level(w)\le level(u)+1$. A forward edge goes from $u$ to a non-child descendant $w$, so $level(w)\ge level(u)+2$ $\text{---}$ this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges $\text{---}$ TRUE. The others can fail: - Back edge: G = {v$\rightarrow$a, a$\rightarrow$v}. Tree {v$\rightarrow$a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a$\rightarrow$v is a back edge. - Cross edge: G = {v$\rightarrow$a, v$\rightarrow$b, b$\rightarrow$a}. DFS visits a then b; b$\rightarrow$a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree. - So G can also have edges outside T.

go:422806.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 36
go:422806.question:
​​​​Consider the following read-write schedule $\text{S}$ over three transactions $T_{1}, T_{2}$, and $T_{3}$, where the subscripts in the schedule indicate transaction IDs:

$S: r_{1}(z) ; w_{1}(z) ; r_{2}(x) ; r_{3}(y) ; w_{3}(y) ; r_{2}(y) ; w_{2}(x) ; w_{2}(y) ;$

Which of the following transaction schedules is/are conflict equivalent to $\text{S}$?

  1. $T_{1} T_{2} T_{3}$
  2. $T_{1} T_{3} T_{2}$
  3. $T_{3} T_{2} T_{1}$
  4. $T_{3} T_{1} T_{2}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write): - z: only T1 uses it $\rightarrow$ T1 has no conflict with anyone. - x: only T2 uses it. - y: $r_3(y),w_3(y)$ come before $r_2(y),w_2(y)$ $\rightarrow$ T3 must come before T2. So any serial order with T3 before T2 is conflict equivalent, and T1 can be anywhere: $T_1T_3T_2,\;T_3T_2T_1,\;T_3T_1T_2$. $T_1T_2T_3$ puts T2 before T3 $\rightarrow$ not equivalent.

go:422805.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 37
go:422805.question:
Consider a Boolean expression given by $\text{F(X, Y, Z)}=\sum(3,5,6,7)$.

Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

  1. $\text{F(X, Y, Z)}=\Pi(0,1,2,4)$ 
  2. $\text{F(X, Y, Z)=X Y+Y Z+X Z}$
  3. $\text{F(X, Y, Z)}$ is independent of input $\text{Y}$
  4. $\text{F(X, Y, Z)}$ is independent of input $\text{X}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Minterms 3, 5, 6, 7 = 011, 101, 110, 111 $\rightarrow$ F = 1 when at least two inputs are 1 (majority function).

- Maxterms are the remaining combinations: $\Pi(0,1,2,4)$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- Majority function $=XY+YZ+XZ$ $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- Depends on Y: $F(1,0,0)=0$ but $F(1,1,0)=1$ $\text{---}$ so not independent of Y.

- Depends on X: $F(0,1,0)=0$ but $F(1,1,0)=1$ $\text{---}$ so not independent of X.

go:422804.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 38
go:422804.question:
​​Consider the following $\mathrm{C}$ function definition.

int f (int x, int y){
for (int i=0 ; i<y ; i++ ) {
x= x + x + y;
}
return x;
}

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the above function?

  1. If the inputs are $x=20, y=10$, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$
  2. If the inputs are $x=20, y=20$, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$
  3. If the inputs are $x=20, y=10$, then the return value is less than $2^{10}$
  4. If the inputs are $x=10, y=20$, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Each iteration does $x\leftarrow2x+y$, repeated $y$ times. Solving:

$f(x,y)=2^y x+(2^y-1)y=2^y(x+y)-y$

- $x=20,y=10$: $1024\times30-10=30710$. This is less than $2^{20}$ but more than $2^{10}$ $\rightarrow$ options 1 and 3 FALSE.

- $x=20,y=20$: $2^{20}\times40-20 \gt 2^{20}$ $\rightarrow$ TRUE.

- $x=10,y=20$: $2^{20}\times30-20 \gt 2^{20}$ $\rightarrow$ TRUE.

(Both values are about $4\times10^7$, so no int overflow.)

go:422803.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 39
go:422803.question:
​​Let $A$ be any $n \times m$ matrix, where $m>n$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations $Ax=0$?

  1. There exist at least $m-n$ linearly independent solutions to this system
  2. There exist $m-n$ linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
  3. There exists a non-zero solution in which at least $m-n$ variables are $0$
  4. There exists a solution in which at least $n$ variables are non-zero

detailed_solution.markdown:
$rank(A)\le n \lt m$, so the solution space has dimension $m-rank(A)\ge m-n$.

- At least $m-n$ linearly independent solutions $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- "$m-n$ vectors span every solution" fails when the dimension is larger, e.g. A = zero matrix (dimension m) $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- $A=[1\;\;1]$ ($n=1,m=2$): solutions are $t(1,-1)$; no non-zero solution has a zero entry, though $m-n=1$ $\text{---}$ FALSE.

- $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}$$: solutions $(0,0,t)$ have only 1 non-zero variable $\lt n=2$ $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:422802.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 40
go:422802.question:
​Consider the $5$ -state $\text{DFA}$. $M$ accepting the language $L(M) \subset(0+1)^{*}$ shown below. For any string $w \in(0+1)^*$ let $n_0(w)$ be the number of $0^{\prime} s$ in $w$ and $n_1(w)$ be the number of 1 's in $w$.

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

  1. States $2$ and $4$ are distinguishable in $M$
  2. States $3$ and $4$ are distinguishable in $M$
  3. States $2$ and $5$ are distinguishable in $M$
  4. Any string $w$ with $n_0(w)=n_1(w)$ is in $L(M)$

detailed_solution.markdown: Reading 0 moves 1$\rightarrow$2$\rightarrow$3$\rightarrow$1, reading 1 moves 1$\rightarrow$4$\rightarrow$5$\rightarrow$1, and the reverse arrows undo a step. So the DFA tracks $(n_0-n_1)\bmod 3$: state 1 = 0, states 2 and 5 = 1, states 3 and 4 = 2. $L(M)=\{w: n_0(w)\equiv n_1(w)\pmod 3\}$, and states with the same value are equivalent. - 2 and 4 (values 1 and 2): distinguishable (input "1": 2$\rightarrow$1 accept, 4$\rightarrow$5 reject) $\text{---}$ TRUE. - 3 and 4: both value 2 $\rightarrow$ equivalent $\text{---}$ statement FALSE. - 2 and 5: both value 1 $\rightarrow$ equivalent $\text{---}$ statement FALSE. - $n_0=n_1$ $\Rightarrow$ difference 0 $\Rightarrow$ accepted $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:422801.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 41
go:422801.question:
​​​The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colours used in a proper colouring of the graph. Let $G$ be any graph with $n$ vertices and chromatic number $k$. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

  1. $G$ contains a complete subgraph with $k$ vertices
  2. $G$ contains an independent set of size at least $n/k$
  3. $G$ contains at least $k(k-1) / 2$ edges
  4. $G$ contains a vertex of degree at least $k$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- Complete subgraph of size k: FALSE. The 5-cycle $C_5$ has $\chi=3$ but no triangle.

- Independent set of size $\ge n/k$: TRUE. The k colour classes are independent sets covering n vertices, so the largest has at least $n/k$ vertices.

- At least $k(k-1)/2$ edges: TRUE. In a minimum colouring, every pair of colour classes must have an edge between them (otherwise merge the two classes and use $k-1$ colours). That gives $\binom{k}{2}$ edges.

- Vertex of degree $\ge k$: FALSE. $K_k$ has $\chi=k$ but every degree is $k-1$.

go:422800.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 42
go:422800.question:
Consider the operators $\diamond$ and $\square$ defined by $a \diamond b=a+2 b, a \square b=a b$, for positive integers. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. Operator $\diamond$ obeys the associative law
  2. Operator $\square$ obeys the associative law
  3. Operator $\diamond$ over the operator $\square$ obeys the distributive law
  4. Operator $\square$ over the operator $\diamond$ obeys the distributive law

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- $\diamond$ associative? $(a\diamond b)\diamond c=a+2b+2c$, $a\diamond(b\diamond c)=a+2b+4c$ $\rightarrow$ NO.

- $\square$ is ordinary multiplication $\rightarrow$ associative, YES.

- $\diamond$ over $\square$: $a\diamond(b\square c)=a+2bc$, but $(a\diamond b)\square(a\diamond c)=(a+2b)(a+2c)$. For $a=b=c=1$: 3 vs 9 $\rightarrow$ NO.

- $\square$ over $\diamond$: $a\square(b\diamond c)=a(b+2c)=ab+2ac=(a\square b)\diamond(a\square c)$ $\rightarrow$ YES.

go:422799.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 43
go:422799.question:
​​​​Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: $\text{WBC}$, which uses the write back policy, and $\text{WTC}$, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use the $\text{LRU}$ (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  1. A read miss in $\text{WBC}$ never evicts a dirty block
  2. A read miss in $\text{WTC}$ never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to main memory
  3. A write hit in $\text{WBC}$ can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block 
  4. A write miss in $\text{WTC}$ always writes the victim cache block to main memory before loading the missed block to the cache

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- WBC read miss: the LRU victim may be dirty and then it must be written back $\text{---}$ FALSE ("never" is wrong).

- WTC read miss: with write-through, memory is always up to date, so a victim never needs to be written back $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- WBC write hit: the block becomes dirty, so the dirty bit can change from 0 to 1 $\text{---}$ TRUE.

- WTC write miss: the victim block is never dirty, so it is never written back $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:422798.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 44
go:422798.question: Consider a $512$ GB hard disk with $32$ storage surfaces. There are $4096$ sectors per track and each sector holds $1024$ bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard disk is _________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Capacity = cylinders $\times$ surfaces $\times$ sectors per track $\times$ bytes per sector.

$512\text{ GB}=2^{39}$, 32 surfaces $=2^5$, 4096 sectors $=2^{12}$, 1024 bytes $=2^{10}$.

Cylinders $=\dfrac{2^{39}}{2^5\times2^{12}\times2^{10}}=2^{12}=4096$

go:422797.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 45
go:422797.question:
The baseline execution time of a program on a $2 \mathrm{GHz}$ single core machine is $100$ nanoseconds ( $n s)$. The code corresponding to $90 \%$ of the execution time can be fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is $10 ~ns$ when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.

The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Serial part $=10\%$ of 100 ns = 10 ns, parallel part = 90 ns.

With $p$ cores: $T(p)=10+\dfrac{90}{p}+10(p-1)$

- $p=1$: 100 ns

- $p=2$: $10+45+10=65$ ns

- $p=3$: $10+30+20=60$ ns

- $p=4$: $10+22.5+30=62.5$ ns

Minimum at $p=3$ (also from $\frac{90}{p}=10p$ $\Rightarrow$ $p=3$).

go:422796.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 46
go:422796.question: A given program has $25 \%$ load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal $\text{CPI}$ (cycles per instruction) without any memory stalls is $2$. The program exhibits $2 \%$ miss rate on instruction cache and $8 \%$ miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is $100$ cycles. The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e., with NO data or instruction cache misses) is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Every instruction is fetched (I-cache) and 25% also access data (D-cache).

Stall cycles per instruction:

- I-cache: $1\times0.02\times100=2$

- D-cache: $0.25\times0.08\times100=2$

Actual CPI $=2+2+2=6$, perfect-cache CPI $=2$.

Speedup $=6/2=3.00$

go:422795.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 47
go:422795.question:
Consider the following code snippet using the fork and wait system calls. Assume that the code compiles and runs correctly, and that the system calls run successfully without any errors.
 

int x=3;

while (x>0){

fork ;

printf("hello");

wait (NULL) ;

X-- ;

}

The total number of times the printf statement is executed is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown: In each iteration every existing process calls fork(), so the number of processes doubles, and each of them prints once. (wait() only changes the order, not the count; each child continues the loop with the current x.) - x = 3: 1 $\rightarrow$ 2 processes, prints 2 - x = 2: 2 $\rightarrow$ 4 processes, prints 4 - x = 1: 4 $\rightarrow$ 8 processes, prints 8 Total $=2+4+8=14$

go:422794.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 48
go:422794.question:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an $\text{IP}$ router. Each entry consists of an $\text{IP}$ prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination $\text{IP}$ address matches the prefix. The notation " /$\mathrm{N}$ " in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant $\mathrm{N}$ bits set to $1$.$$\begin{array}{|ll|ll|} \hline \textbf{Prefix} && \textbf{Next hop router} \\\hline \text{10.1.1.0 / 24} && \text{R1} \\\hline \text{10.1.1.128 / 25}&& \text{R2} \\\hline   \text{10.1.1.64 / 26}&& \text{R3} \\\hline  \text{10.1.1.192 / 26}&& \text{R4} \\\hline \end{array}$$
This router forwards $20$ packets each to $5$ hosts. The $\text{IP}$ addresses of the hosts are $10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191,$ and $10.1.1.205$. The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router $\mathrm{R} 2$ is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown: Use longest prefix match. Address ranges (last byte): /24 $\rightarrow$ 0-255 (R1), .128/25 $\rightarrow$ 128-255 (R2), .64/26 $\rightarrow$ 64-127 (R3), .192/26 $\rightarrow$ 192-255 (R4). - 10.1.1.16 $\rightarrow$ only /24 $\rightarrow$ R1 - 10.1.1.72 $\rightarrow$ /26 (64-127) $\rightarrow$ R3 - 10.1.1.132 $\rightarrow$ /25 $\rightarrow$ R2 - 10.1.1.191 $\rightarrow$ /25 (not in 192-255) $\rightarrow$ R2 - 10.1.1.205 $\rightarrow$ /26 (192-255) $\rightarrow$ R4 R2 gets 2 hosts $\times$ 20 packets $=40$.

go:422793.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 49
go:422793.question: Let $G=(V, \Sigma, S, P)$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with $\Sigma=\{a, b, c\}$ and $V$ containing $10$ variable symbols including the start symbol $S$. The string $w=a^{30} b^{30} c^{30}$ is derivable from $S$. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation $S \rightarrow^* w$ is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
CNF rules are $A\rightarrow BC$ or $A\rightarrow a$.

- Each $A\rightarrow BC$ increases the number of symbols by 1. To grow from 1 symbol (S) to $n$ symbols needs $n-1$ such steps.

- Each of the $n$ variables is then turned into a terminal by $A\rightarrow a$: $n$ steps.

Total $=2n-1$. Here $n=|w|=90$: $2(90)-1=179$.

go:422792.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 50
go:422792.question: The number of edges present in the forest generated by the $\text{DFS}$ traversal of an undirected graph $G$ with $100$ vertices is $40$. The number of connected components in $G$ is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
DFS produces one tree per connected component. A tree with $k$ vertices has $k-1$ edges, so a forest with $n$ vertices and $c$ trees has $n-c$ edges.

$100-c=40\Rightarrow c=60$

go:422791.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 51
go:422791.question:
Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$ :

$r= 0^{*}+1^{*}$

$s = 01^{*} + 10^{*}$

The total number of strings of length less than or equal to $5$, which are neither in $r$ nor in $s$, is ________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Total strings of length 0 to 5: $1+2+4+8+16+32=63$.

- $r=0^*+1^*$: $\epsilon$, plus all-0 and all-1 strings of each length 1-5: $1+2\times5=11$.

- $s=01^*+10^*$: for each length 1-5, the strings $01\ldots1$ and $10\ldots0$. Length 1 ("0", "1") is already in r, so new ones = $2\times4=8$.

In r or s: $11+8=19$. Neither: $63-19=44$.

go:422790.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 52
go:422790.question: Consider a memory management system that uses a page size of $2 \mathrm{~KB}$. Assume that both the physical and virtual addresses start from $0$. Assume that the pages $0,1,2$, and $3$ are stored in the page frames $1,3,2$, and $0$, respectively. The physical address (in decimal format) corresponding to the virtual address $2500$ (in decimal format) is ___________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Page size $=2\text{ KB}=2048$.

$2500=1\times2048+452$ $\rightarrow$ page 1, offset 452.

Page 1 is in frame 3.

Physical address $=3\times2048+452=6144+452=6596$

go:422789.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 53
go:422789.question: A bag contains $10$ red balls and $15$ blue balls. Two balls are drawn randomly without replacement. Given that the first ball drawn is red, the probability (rounded off to $3$ decimal places) that both balls drawn are red is ___________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Given the first ball is red, 9 red and 15 blue (24 balls) remain. Both are red iff the second is red:

$P=\dfrac{P(\text{both red})}{P(\text{first red})}=\dfrac{\frac{10}{25}\cdot\frac{9}{24}}{\frac{10}{25}}=\dfrac{9}{24}=0.375$

go:422788.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 54
go:422788.question:
Consider a digital logic circuit consisting of three $2$-to-$1$ multiplexers $\text{M1, M2}$, and $\text{M3}$ as shown below. $\mathrm{X} 1$ and $\mathrm{X} 2$ are inputs of $\mathrm{M} 1$. $\text{X3}$ and $\text{X4}$ are inputs of $\text{M2}$. $\text{A, B}$, and $\text{C}$ are select lines of $\text{M1, M2}$, and $\text{M3}$, respectively.

For an instance of inputs $\mathbf{X} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{X} \mathbf{2}=\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{X} \mathbf{3}=\mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbf{X} \mathbf{4}=\mathbf{0}$, the number of combinations of $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}$ that give the output $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{1}$ is ____________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Look at each multiplexer separately:

- M1: both inputs $X1=X2=1$, so $Q1=1$ whatever A is.

- M2: both inputs $X3=X4=0$, so $Q2=0$ whatever B is.

- M3: $Y=Q1=1$ when $C=0$, and $Y=Q2=0$ when $C=1$.

So $Y=1$ exactly when $C=0$; A and B are free: $2\times2=4$ combinations.

go:422787.title: GATE CSE 2024 | Set 1 | Question: 55
go:422787.question: Consider sending an $\text{IP}$ datagram of size $1420$ bytes (including $20$ bytes of $\text{IP}$ header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an $\text{MTU}$ (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of $542$ bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an $\text{MTU}$ size of $360$ bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ____________.

detailed_solution.markdown: Data in datagram $=1420-20=1400$ bytes. Fragment data (except the last) must be a multiple of 8. Link 1 (MTU 542): max data $=522$ $\rightarrow$ use 520. Fragments: 520, 520, 360. Link 2 (MTU 360): max data $=340$ $\rightarrow$ use 336. - 520 $\rightarrow$ 336 + 184 - 520 $\rightarrow$ 336 + 184 - 360 $\rightarrow$ 336 + 24 Fragments are reassembled only at the receiver, so it receives $2+2+2=6$ fragments.
